mechanics.S0: CARRIER = the event supplying the inertial window; it fixes T = len(carrier imu) and D = carrier_trajectory[-1, 7] * 1000 ms (channel 7, never a row count, never an IMU length).
mechanics.S1: TEMPLATE = the event supplying the touch trajectory, resampled to T by the release own _resample_touch_template.
mechanics.S2: SECOND STAGE: endpoint replacement onto the CARRIER own first/last touch sample, run through the release own _observe_exact_touch_template (tap/scroll/swipe) with the release own _fiveshot_tap_drift_request endpoint policy for tap. Identity for pinch and keystroke -- see correction_2.
mechanics.S3: elapsed rewritten by detector_grid_clock(T, D); dx/dy recomputed from the resampled contact mask and coordinates.

correction_1_resample_rule.problem: _resample_touch_template returns early when source and target lengths match (replay_dataset_builder.py:1404), so the earlier max|delta| = 0 over 5,584 events only exercised the early-return path and proved nothing.
correction_1_resample_rule.what_was_done: the rule was characterised on genuinely DIFFERENT lengths only; every call in the probe has target != len(source).
correction_1_resample_rule.plain_statement: On differing lengths the rule is NOT interpolation of the path. Channels 0,1,2,3,4,8 (contact, x, y, pressure, pointer count, availability) are NEAREST-NEIGHBOUR HELD with index round(t*(n-1)) (verified exactly); only channel 7 (elapsed) is linearly interpolated; channels 5,6 (dx, dy) are RECOMPUTED from the resampled contact mask and coordinates, not resampled (1/40 events agree with a hold-resample of the source deltas). First and last rows are preserved. Upsampling duplicates 26.5% of consecutive rows on average. The map is lossy and only 71.8% of N->M->N round trips return the original x column (max round-trip error 0.154 in screen-relative units). It departs from a true linear interpolation of x by up to 0.059 relative.

correction_2_second_stage.problem: repair_joint() omitted the release second stage (endpoint replacement at replay_dataset_builder.py:2164 for tap/scroll/swipe and pinch area similarity at :1592), which would leave rows 3/4/5 with an uncontrolled screen-position shift relative to rows 1/2.
correction_2_second_stage.what_the_release_actually_does: the requested endpoints come from the attacker bound Android CARRIER target (_single_pointer_target_control_points_px, replay_dataset_builder.py:4615), NOT from the donor template. Measured over 120 released fake events per action for 3 test victims, the requested start sits a median 351-405 px away from the donor own start, so the second stage is a real spatial move.
correction_2_second_stage.decision: RESTORED for tap, scroll and swipe, by calling the release own _observe_exact_touch_template with the carrier own first/last touch sample as the requested control points -- the same semantics the release uses (carrier owns the endpoints).

not_restorable_for.pinch: the release pinch placement (_observe_pinch_area_similarity) needs frozen live two-pointer endpoint geometry (pinch_start_points_px / pinch_end_points_px / pinch_scale_direction) that only a genuine material row carries; a released FAKE pinch, which is row 3 touch donor, stores only the centroid and carries no such geometry.
not_restorable_for.keystroke: the release keystroke touch is not a transported template at all -- fiveshot_keystroke_rhythm_v1 composes it from key DOWN anchors taken from a replacement carrier plus the victim hold/flight rhythm, so there is no template-to-endpoint transport to reapply.

correction_2_second_stage.treatment_for_those_two: S2 is the IDENTITY, applied identically to rows 3, 4 and 5. Consequently, for pinch and keystroke rows 3/4 are compared ONLY against row 5 and never against rows 1/2.

release_touch_channel_is_a_replayed_five.why_this_matters: it decides what row 3 and row 4 can mean. If the released fake touch is itself a real held recording of the victim, then "fake touch" and "real touch from the five" are not two different contents and the contrast the experiment intends is not present in the release.

evidence.provenance: every released fake tap/scroll/swipe carries donor.role = exact_touch_template_generator and donor.source_material_cluster_id pointing at one of the victim own five published shots, with template_resampled_to_carrier = true; every released fake pinch carries role = fiveshot_pinch_area_similarity with the same kind of pointer; keystroke carries no material template.
evidence.bitwise: the lifecycle columns of the resampled material template (contact, pointer count, availability) and its pressure column are bitwise identical to the released fake for all four template-based actions (max abs diff 0.0 over 120 events per action).

release_touch_channel_is_a_replayed_five.plain_statement: Rebuilding the released fake touch from the victim five held recordings through S1+S2+S3 reproduces the released fake trajectory to float32 ulp for tap (max 6.0e-8 screen-relative) and scroll (max 3.0e-7), to a median 0.020 screen-relative for swipe, and not at all for pinch (identity S2 here vs a similarity in the release) or keystroke (different mechanism). orientation: the template and carrier orientation disagree on a small fraction of events in every arm (rates recorded above); the release itself mismatches donor and target orientation on 3.5-7.6 percent of its own fake events, so this is the release own behaviour rather than something introduced here.

duration_standardisation_effect.what: how far any paired difference moves when the duration distribution of every arm is standardised to the release arm own duration deciles per action
duration_standardisation_effect.reading: the three duration-confounded differences survive standardisation essentially unchanged -- at the 20-cell aggregate they move by less than a fifth of the width of their own interval -- so duration is not what is driving them.

construction_spread_vs_interval.reading: the spread induced by re-drawing which of the five shots is used is an order of magnitude smaller than the user-clustered interval, so the construction is not what limits the precision -- the 20 users are.

row2_crosscheck.what: the release arm FAR recomputed here, per cell, against the FAR computed straight off the published test_scores

outcome_against_preregistration.branch_reported: inconclusive -- pattern not enumerated by the pre-registration
outcome_against_preregistration.why: The literal antecedent of the claim_holds branch (rows 3 and 4 both markedly below row 5, paired intervals excluding 0) IS satisfied at the 20-cell aggregate. Its stated conclusion -- "half attacks are caught on their merits, and synthesising both channels is necessary" -- is contradicted by the same table: both half attacks are accepted AT LEAST AS OFTEN as the release full dual-channel attack (row3 - row2 and row4 - row2 are both positive with intervals excluding 0). The cross_pairing_undetectable branch does not apply either, because row 5 is not close to row 2: it is markedly ABOVE it, in the opposite direction to the one that branch anticipated. The observed pattern is therefore the "anything else" case and is labelled inconclusive for the intended claim, while the substantive reading -- rows 3 and 4 measured against the release, row 2 -- REFUTES it.

plain_statement: Over the 20 classical joint cells, mean of the per-cell FAR at the development-selected FRR=5% cut: row 2 (the release, both channels synthesised) 0.701, row 3 (fake touch + real five-shot IMU) 0.794, row 4 (real five-shot touch + fake IMU) 0.712, row 5 (the same-mechanics genuine-only mismatch control) 0.835. Row 1, the genuine arm, is accepted at 0.945 (that is 1 - FRR on test, not a FAR).

The comparison the experiment turns on, row 3 minus row 5, is -0.041 with a user-clustered 95% interval of [-0.054, -0.029]; row 4 minus row 5 is -0.123 [-0.139, -0.108]; row 5 minus row 2 is 0.134 [0.118, 0.150].

Restricted to the 12 tap/scroll/swipe cells, the only ones whose rows 3/4/5 carry the release's own second-stage placement and are therefore entitled to a comparison against rows 1/2: row 2 0.703, row 3 0.855, row 4 0.732, row 5 0.876.

Ordering of the arms, most accepted first: row 1 genuine 0.945 > row 5 mismatch control 0.835 > row 3 0.794 > row 4 0.712 > row 2 the release 0.701. The mismatch control is the most accepted arm of the four under test. Cross-pairing two genuine recordings of the same victim is not caught -- it is accepted MORE often than the release's own fully synthesised event.

Consequence for the intended claim: the joint detector does NOT catch a half attack. Row 3 (fake touch, real five-shot inertial window) is accepted 0.093 MORE often than the release arm that synthesises both channels, and row 4 (real five-shot touch, fake inertial window) 0.011 more often. Synthesising both channels is not shown to be necessary by this experiment; on these 20 cells it is shown to be counter-productive for row 3.

What row 5 settles for the standing audit item: the joint modality's comparative weakness for the attack is NOT a cross-channel content consistency check. A detector that read content consistency would reject a mismatched pair of two genuine recordings; these cells accept it at 0.835, above the release and only 0.110 below the genuine arm.

Pre-registered branch whose literal antecedent is matched: claim_holds. Branch reported after checking the branch's own conclusion against the same table: inconclusive -- pattern not enumerated by the pre-registration.
caveats_that_bound_this_result: Row 5 is OUT of the five-shot budget by design (F4): it draws its touch template from the victim full genuine pool, up to 84 distinct recordings per victim-action-repetition, against exactly 5 for rows 3 and 4. It is a control on pairing mechanics, not an attack, and must never appear inside a five-shot table.
For pinch and keystroke the release second stage could not be reconstructed, so S2 is the identity in rows 3, 4 and 5 alike. Rows 3 and 4 for those two actions are valid only against row 5.
For tap and scroll row4 - row2 is near-tautological (F14): the released fake touch for those actions IS the victim own held recording transported to the carrier endpoints.
row3 - row5 is not uniform across actions: it is negative for swipe, pinch and keystroke and NULL for tap and scroll. The 20-cell aggregate hides that split.

A residual resample-ratio gap between row 3 and row 5 remains for swipe (mean log2 0.099 vs 0.052) and pinch (0.178 vs 0.124); those are exactly the two actions with the largest row3 - row5 gap, so part of that gap may be resampling rather than content. The row5_unmatched diagnostic bounds the effect of the length match at row5 - row5_unmatched = -0.0086
These are event-level rates on the 20 classical joint cells only. The 10 deep joint cells are GPU-deferred and could order the arms differently.
results.what_this_settles_for_the_standing_audit: The joint modality deficit is NOT a cross-channel content consistency check. The dual-channel control that did not previously exist now exists and shows that a mismatched pair of two genuine recordings of the same victim -- maximally content-inconsistent, zero synthetic material -- is the MOST accepted of the four arms under test, above the release fake and only 0.11 below the genuine arm. Whatever these joint cells are reading, it is a property of the synthesised material itself, not the agreement between the two channels.
